screens.title: Version Control with Perforce/Git for Game Projects
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn why version control is an essential safety net for game development and how to put an Unreal Engine project under Git. We'll cover the core reasons teams use version control, practical steps to initialize a repository, protect generated files with a. gitignore, and basic workflows for staging, committing, pushing, and pulling changes. You will also learn collaboration basics: creating branches, merging, and resolving conflicts when binary assets are involved. A concrete example we'll revisit is creating a small Blueprint actor, saving it, and committing it to your repository so you can see history and roll back if needed. We'll contrast Git with Perforce at a high level so you know which tool suits your team. Finally, I'll emphasize safety practices like frequent small commits, using Git LFS for large binaries, and stashing or committing before you pull. By the end, you should be able to initialize Git, create a sensible. gitignore for Unreal, and perform the everyday commands that keep your project safe and collaborative.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on practical competencies you can demonstrate. First, you'll understand the principles and benefits of version control for game projects, which means you can explain why teams need a reliable history and how that history protects work and enables collaboration. Second, you'll set up a basic Git repository at the Unreal project's root and create a working. gitignore so generated files are not tracked. Third, you'll perform essential Git operations: staging changes, committing meaningful messages, and pushing and pulling to a remote repository so your work is shared and backed up. Fourth, you'll collaborate using branches: create a feature branch, integrate work with merges, and handle conflicts that arise, especially for Unreal binary assets. Each objective is paired with a small verification milestone so you can confirm you performed the steps. Together these skills let you comfortably manage source for a small team or solo Unreal project while avoiding common pitfalls like committing build artifacts or losing uncommitted work.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical application. You'll learn to use. gitignore correctly so the repository stays lean and avoids generated files that differ per machine. You'll also become fluent with remote operations: linking a remote repository and pushing your commits for remote backup and team sharing. Finally, you'll understand how to handle binary merge conflicts and when to use file locks or coordinate edits to prevent them. These are the habits that keep a game's source manageable over months of development.

screens.title: Why Version Control is Critical in Game Development
screens.narratorSegment: Version control systems record every change to your project so you can return to a previous state if something breaks. In game development, this is more than convenience. Large projects evolve over months, many files change at once, and binary assets make conflicts costly. A VCS gives you a history of who changed what and when, and it enables branching to isolate risky experiments. For example, if a teammate adds a new enemy Blueprint and it introduces a bug, you can inspect recent commits to find when the bug appeared or revert to the commit before the change. A common misconception is that version control is only for code; in game teams it's equally important for Blueprints, materials, and scene changes. However, binary assets such as compiled Blueprints require different handling because they do not merge automatically. That means you need habits: commit frequently, use small descriptive messages, and coordinate when editing large binary files. The core takeaway is simple: version control turns accidental deletions or regressions into solvable, trackable events rather than project disasters. Why Version Control is Critical in Game Development means it provides recoverability, clear history, and collaborative workflows that reduce risk and enable teams to work in parallel.. In practical terms, protect your work, enable collaboration, and trace changes over time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Why VCS is Critical
Definition and benefits

A version control system records changes to files and allows you to inspect, compare, and revert those changes. For teams, it prevents accidental overwrites and provides a shared history.

  • Recover previous states after a bad commit or accidental deletion.
  • Trace who changed assets and why using commit messages.
  • Work in parallel using branches to avoid stepping on teammates' work.
Concrete example: create BP_Door, save, close editor, then run git add and git commit. You now have a snapshot you can return to if future edits break the door behavior.
Common mistake: assuming binaries merge like text. Two people editing the same .uasset will cause a conflict requiring one version to be chosen.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Version control converts accidental loss into a recoverable event and enables parallel work without destructive overwrites.

Why it matters: your project's history is the most important artifact after the game itself.

screens.title: Perforce vs Git for Game Projects
screens.narratorSegment: Perforce and Git are both used in game development, but they suit different team needs. Perforce has historically been chosen by large studios because it handles large binary files well and supports exclusive file locking. That means artists can lock a binary asset like a texture so nobody else accidentally edits the same file at the same time. Git, by contrast, is distributed and flexible; it excels for smaller teams or indie projects where contributors may work offline and push when ready. Git needs extensions like Git LFS to store large binary assets efficiently. A common misconception is that Git cannot be used for games; in practice, many teams use Git with Git LFS successfully, especially when combined with good branching practices and communication. The practical decision rests on team size, asset size, and whether exclusive locking is required. For many beginner projects, Git plus Git LFS provides an approachable workflow. For larger teams handling many large binaries and complex locking needs, Perforce may simplify coordination at scale. Perforce vs Git for Game Projects means perforce offers centralized locking and binary handling; git is distributed and flexible and gains binary support via git lfs.. In practical terms, high-level trade-offs studios consider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Perforce vs Git
Perforce (studio scale)
  • Handles very large binary stores efficiently.
  • Supports file locking to prevent simultaneous edits of binaries.
  • Often used where centralized control and strict locks are preferred.
Scenario: A 50-person art team uses exclusive checkout for large texture libraries so only one artist edits a given texture at a time.
Git + Git LFS (small/indie)
  • Distributed commits and offline work. Each developer has a full history locally.
  • Git LFS stores pointers to large files and keeps the repository lightweight.
  • File locking is possible with LFS, but coordination and branching are typical strategies.
Scenario: A small studio uses Git with Git LFS and communicates in tasks to avoid simultaneous edits of the same asset.
Practical guidance
For beginner projects, start with Git and Git LFS. If your team scales and needs centralized locking or specific binary workflows, evaluate Perforce. Regardless, adopt habits: small commits, clear messages, and coordinate edits to avoid merge conflicts on binaries.

screens.title: Initialize a Git Repository for Your Unreal Project
screens.narratorSegment: Initializing a repository is the gate that gives you history and backups. Start by opening a terminal and navigating to the folder that contains your. uproject file. Running the initialization command creates a. git directory that will store commit history. A common novice mistake is running git init in the wrong folder and ending up with a repository that doesn't include your Content folder. Once the. gitignore exists, stage files with git add then commit with a clear message such as Initial project setup. A practical example: navigate to C colon slash UnrealProjects slash MyNewGame, run git init, create. gitignore with the lines given in this module, then git add. and git commit. That sequence gives you a clean initial snapshot. Always confirm by running git status and git log to verify your repository state. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Initialize Git
Terminal steps
cd C:\UnrealProjects\MyAwesomeGame
git init
# create .gitignore with Unreal entries
git add .
git commit -m "Initial project setup and basic level created"
  • Confirm location: check that your .uproject file is in the current directory before running git init.
  • Create .gitignore before adding files so generated files remain untracked.
  • Use clear commit messages describing the snapshot.
Example
You initialize in MyAwesomeGame, add a minimal .gitignore, then commit. Running git log shows your initial commit and commit message. If you later create a new Blueprint and commit it, you'll see both snapshots in the history.
Key Takeaway

Initialize at the .uproject root, create .gitignore, then add and commit to capture a clean baseline.

screens.title: Creating a .gitignore for Unreal Engine
screens.narratorSegment: A. gitignore file tells Git which files and directories to ignore so they are not tracked. For Unreal Engine projects, many directories are machine-specific or derived: Binaries, Build, DerivedDataCache, Intermediate, and Saved are examples. If you commit these folders you will dramatically increase repository size and create merge noise that slows everyone down. Create a. gitignore at the project root with those entries and common IDE files such as Visual Studio solutions. A simple example provided in this chapter is sufficient for a beginner project. A frequently made mistake is adding. gitignore after those files have already been committed; in that case you'll need to remove them from the index and commit the removal. Also remember: ignoring files does not delete them locally; it only stops tracking new changes. Practical tip: verify your. gitignore with git status before committing. Confirm the Content folder and. uproject files are included so your project assets are tracked while generated files remain out of source control. Creating a .gitignore for Unreal Engine means it keeps generated and machine-specific files out of the repo so history remains small and merges stay manageable.. In practical terms, prevent generated files from bloating your repository. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › .gitignore
Minimal Unreal .gitignore
# Unreal Engine generated files
.vs/
Binaries/
Build/
DerivedDataCache/
Intermediate/
Saved/
*.VC.db
*.opensdf
*.sdf
*.sln
*.suo
*.user
*.xcodeproj
*.xcworkspace
If you added generated files before creating .gitignore, remove them from tracking with git rm --cached and commit that removal. The file keeps your repository fast and reduces conflict frequency.
Common mistake
Committing Binaries or Intermediate folders before ignoring them. This bloat is hard to undo and slows clones and operations.
Action
Create .gitignore first, then git add and git commit. If you must remove tracked generated files, use git rm --cached <file> and commit the removal.

screens.title: Staging and Committing Changes
screens.narratorSegment: Staging and committing are the way you create meaningful snapshots of your work. Staging selects which changes will be part of the next commit; committing records that snapshot with a message. A typical sequence is make changes in Unreal, close the editor, run git status to see modified files, git add to stage, and git commit with a descriptive message. For example, after adding a Blueprint called BP_Door and saving it, git status will list Content slash Blueprints slash BP_Door. uasset. You might run git add Content/Blueprints/BP_Door. uasset and then git commit -m "Add BP_Door actor with static mesh". Avoid committing everything blindly with git add. unless your. gitignore is correct; selective staging helps produce focused commits that explain a single logical change. A common misconception is that bigger commits are better — the opposite is true: small, frequent commits make history easier to read and make it simpler to revert or bisect problems later. Staging and Committing Changes means stage deliberate changes and write clear, focused commit messages to build a useful project history.. In practical terms, how to create clear snapshots of your project. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Staging & Committing
Terminal example
git status
# see new file: Content/Blueprints/BP_Door.uasset

git add Content/Blueprints/BP_Door.uasset

git commit -m "Add BP_Door actor with StaticMesh component"

git log --oneline
  • Run git status frequently to review what will be committed.
  • Prefer staging specific files to keep commits focused and reversible.
  • Close Unreal Editor before committing .uasset files to avoid partial writes.
Example card
You add a door Blueprint and commit it. Later, if the door breaks, check git log to find the commit and use git revert or checkout to restore a working version.
Key Takeaway

Stage intentionally and commit small, descriptive changes to maintain a useful history.

screens.title: Connect to a Remote and Push Your Work
screens.narratorSegment: A remote repository is how you back up work and share changes. After creating a repository on a hosting service, link it to your local repository with git remote add origin followed by the remote URL. Pushing uploads your commits. The first push usually sets the upstream branch using git push -u origin master or main. Once an upstream is set, future pushes are simpler. A practical workflow: create the remote, then run git remote add origin remote-URL, then git push -u origin master. If other team members are already working, fetch or pull first to avoid divergent histories. Understand that pushing does not overwrite other people's work unless you force push. A common beginner mistake is pushing large generated files because. gitignore was missing; avoid that by verifying the tracked files with git status before push. The benefit: remote pushes provide off-site backups and enable teammates to collaborate by pulling your commits. Connect to a Remote and Push Your Work means link a remote, push your initial commits with upstream set, and verify you aren't pushing ignored generated files.. In practical terms, share your commits to a remote host for backup and collaboration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Pulling, Stashing, and Safe Updates
screens.narratorSegment: When working with a team, you'll regularly pull changes others have pushed. Before pulling, it's important to secure your local work. If you have uncommitted changes, either commit them or use git stash to save them temporarily. Stashing stores your modifications in a stack so you can pull and then reapply them. If you pull with uncommitted work, Git may refuse or create a messy merge. A typical safe workflow is git status to check for local changes, git stash save with a short description if needed, git pull origin master to get updates, then git stash pop to reapply your work and resolve any conflicts. Remember: stash is not a substitute for commits; commit frequently so history shows logical changes. A common misconception is that stashing is permanent — it is temporary and intended for short-term work while you sync. If you risk losing changes, prefer committing to a feature branch before pulling. screens.title: Handling Merge Conflicts and Binary Assets
screens.narratorSegment: Merge conflicts occur when Git cannot automatically reconcile changes from two histories. Text files often merge automatically, but binary assets used by Unreal Engine, such as. uasset, cannot be merged line by line. When two people modify the same binary, Git will signal a conflict and you must choose one version. Typical practice is to avoid simultaneous edits of the same asset via task assignment, or to use file locking if your workflow supports it. Git LFS offers optional file locking for large files, and Perforce provides an exclusive checkout model. If you encounter a binary conflict, communicate with your teammate to determine which version to accept and preserve any unique work before committing. A useful habit is to make smaller, more frequent commits and coordinate edits for important binary resources. Finally, always close the Unreal Editor before committing. uasset files to reduce the chance of partial or corrupted writes that complicate merges. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Merge Conflicts
Why merges fail for binaries

Text can merge because differences can be combined line by line. Binary formats are opaque, so automatic merging is impossible. When Git flags a conflict on a .uasset, you will typically pick one version: "take theirs" or "take yours." That choice can lose work if not coordinated.

  • Coordinate edits via tasks or communication to avoid overlapping work on binaries.
  • Use file locking where available to prevent simultaneous edits.
  • Before resolving, export or copy any unique data you want to preserve if possible.
Practical options
Use Git LFS locking, switch to Perforce for enterprise locking, or simply organize tasks so only one person edits a given binary at a time.
Common mistake

Attempting to auto-merge binaries or editing .uasset files while the editor is open can create corrupt or partial files.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn why version control is an essential safety net for game development and how to put an Unreal Engine project under Git. We'll cover the core reasons teams use version control, practical steps to initialize a repository, protect generated files with a. gitignore, and basic workflows for staging, committing, pushing, and pulling changes. You will also learn collaboration basics: creating branches, merging, and resolving conflicts when binary assets are involved. A concrete example we'll revisit is creating a small Blueprint actor, saving it, and committing it to your repository so you can see history and roll back if needed. We'll contrast Git with Perforce at a high level so you know which tool suits your team. Finally, I'll emphasize safety practices like frequent small commits, using Git LFS for large binaries, and stashing or committing before you pull. By the end, you should be able to initialize Git, create a sensible. gitignore for Unreal, and perform the everyday commands that keep your project safe and collaborative.

In this lesson we focus on practical competencies you can demonstrate. First, you'll understand the principles and benefits of version control for game projects, which means you can explain why teams need a reliable history and how that history protects work and enables collaboration. Second, you'll set up a basic Git repository at the Unreal project's root and create a working. gitignore so generated files are not tracked. Third, you'll perform essential Git operations: staging changes, committing meaningful messages, and pushing and pulling to a remote repository so your work is shared and backed up. Fourth, you'll collaborate using branches: create a feature branch, integrate work with merges, and handle conflicts that arise, especially for Unreal binary assets. Each objective is paired with a small verification milestone so you can confirm you performed the steps. Together these skills let you comfortably manage source for a small team or solo Unreal project while avoiding common pitfalls like committing build artifacts or losing uncommitted work.

These objectives focus on practical application. You'll learn to use. gitignore correctly so the repository stays lean and avoids generated files that differ per machine. You'll also become fluent with remote operations: linking a remote repository and pushing your commits for remote backup and team sharing. Another critical skill is safely updating your local copy: pulling other people's changes and using stashing or committing to avoid losing local work. Finally, you'll understand how to handle binary merge conflicts and when to use file locks or coordinate edits to prevent them. Each objective closes the loop between a command and a real-world reason: for example, ignoring Binaries prevents your repo from becoming hundreds of megabytes of build artifacts, and frequent small commits make it straightforward to bisect regressions. These are the habits that keep a game's source manageable over months of development.

Version control systems record every change to your project so you can return to a previous state if something breaks. In game development, this is more than convenience. Large projects evolve over months, many files change at once, and binary assets make conflicts costly. A VCS gives you a history of who changed what and when, and it enables branching to isolate risky experiments. For example, if a teammate adds a new enemy Blueprint and it introduces a bug, you can inspect recent commits to find when the bug appeared or revert to the commit before the change. A common misconception is that version control is only for code; in game teams it's equally important for Blueprints, materials, and scene changes. However, binary assets such as compiled Blueprints require different handling because they do not merge automatically. That means you need habits: commit frequently, use small descriptive messages, and coordinate when editing large binary files. The core takeaway is simple: version control turns accidental deletions or regressions into solvable, trackable events rather than project disasters. Perforce and Git are both used in game development, but they suit different team needs. Perforce has historically been chosen by large studios because it handles large binary files well and supports exclusive file locking. That means artists can lock a binary asset like a texture so nobody else accidentally edits the same file at the same time. Git, by contrast, is distributed and flexible; it excels for smaller teams or indie projects where contributors may work offline and push when ready. Git needs extensions like Git LFS to store large binary assets efficiently. A common misconception is that Git cannot be used for games; in practice, many teams use Git with Git LFS successfully, especially when combined with good branching practices and communication. The practical decision rests on team size, asset size, and whether exclusive locking is required. For many beginner projects, Git plus Git LFS provides an approachable workflow. For larger teams handling many large binaries and complex locking needs, Perforce may simplify coordination at scale. Merge conflicts occur when Git cannot automatically reconcile changes from two histories. Text files often merge automatically, but binary assets used by Unreal Engine, such as. uasset, cannot be merged line by line. When two people modify the same binary, Git will signal a conflict and you must choose one version. Typical practice is to avoid simultaneous edits of the same asset via task assignment, or to use file locking if your workflow supports it. Git LFS offers optional file locking for large files, and Perforce provides an exclusive checkout model. If you encounter a binary conflict, communicate with your teammate to determine which version to accept and preserve any unique work before committing. A useful habit is to make smaller, more frequent commits and coordinate edits for important binary resources.
